items.stem: Why must a workbook containing macros be saved with the .xlsm extension?

options.text: The standard .xlsx format cannot store macro code
options.rationale: Correct: macro code requires the macro-enabled .xlsm format.
The extension is about storing macros, not speed.

options.text: Because VBA only runs on Windows files
options.rationale: The extension requirement is about format, not platform.
.xlsx can contain charts; the issue is macro storage.

items.explanation: Correct: macro code requires the macro-enabled .xlsm format.

items.stem: Which TWO are good practices in Excel VBA? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Reference ranges directly instead of using Select then Selection
options.rationale: Correct: direct references are faster and more reliable.

options.text: Declare variables with Dim and an explicit type
options.rationale: Correct: explicit typing catches errors and documents intent.

options.text: Put all logic in a single long Sub for simplicity
options.rationale: Large monolithic subs are harder to maintain and reuse.

options.text: Rely on the macro recorder's code without refactoring
options.rationale: Recorded code is literal and usually needs refactoring.

items.explanation: Correct: direct references are faster and more reliable.

items.stem: In VBA, which statement sets a Range object variable to A1:D5 on Sheet1?

options.rationale: Correct: object variables are assigned with Set and a Range reference.
Assigning an object without Set raises an error.
Dim declares; it does not assign a value on the same line this way.
Let assigns values, not object references, and a string is not a Range.
